messages.subject: Use adapt_diag_e_nuts outside of Stan
messages.subject_clean: Use adapt_diag_e_nuts outside of Stan
messages.body_plain:
I would like to use the really nice adaptive NUTS sampler with a non-Stan model.  The model itself uses a deep learning framework as well as Markov random fields, so it would be painful to port to the Stan language.  I should be able to use the adapt_diag_e_nuts class for the sampling, but I need to provide a valid Model class.

Is the interface for a Model class documented anywhere?  It is unfortunately a template parameter everywhere, so there is no base class.

Thanks,
John

messages.body_plain:
John:

To channel Bob and Michael and maybe Aki too:  It sounds like the resulting posterior distributions will have all sorts of nooks and crannies, so maybe MCMC is not the best way to go.  Maybe something like EP would work better.

That said, I'm a big fan of trying MCMC to see how it will work.  I recommend multiple chains, with starting points taken from different places in the target distributon, so you can get a good idea of mixing.

I don't know anything about the model class stuff, but I guess the Stan coders will know the answer to this one.

Andrew

messages.body_plain:
What Andrew said.  You won't be able to scale full Bayes
effectively over something like deep learning---the posterior's
too multimodal.

Here's the doc for what a model needs to implement:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Model-Concept

We'll be cleaning this up before Stan 3.

One way to go is to write your own function for your log density
and gradients then call that in a one-liner from Stan:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/math/wiki/Adding-a-new-function-with-known-gradients

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Likelihood function marginalized in multilevel IRT model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Likelihood function marginalized in multilevel IRT model
messages.body_plain:
Let me try to reformulate.

Suppose you have observations y, parameters theta, and a latent parameter
z[i] for each observation y[i].   How do you compute the likelihood
p(y | theta)?   Stan lets you draw from the posterior p(theta | y).  Then
how do you calculate the likelihood p(y | theta).  Sure, we know

  p(y | theta) = p(y, z | theta) / p(z | theta).

but that just requires us to compute p(z | theta), which I think is
the integral in question here.

I still think Aki and Andrew are the one's the one to ask about
this!

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Use adapt_diag_e_nuts outside of Stan
messages.body_plain:
To be fair, I am not planning to use NUTS on the neural network parameters themselves.  I have a trained variational autoencoder (a la Kingma and Welling https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114) using PyTorch to handle the deep learning model.  The parameters on which I will do HMC are the latent dimensions of the autoencoder.  I expect that this space should be clean enough by construction of the autoencoder, otherwise the gaussian variational posterior would not achieve a good entropy bound.  In the worst case, I might need parallel tempering (which I assume Stan doesn't have).

It would be really nice if Stan's MCMC engine were split out into a proper library that could be used outside of Stan.  Please correct me if I am wrong, but is it as simple as writing a virtual base class that implements the Model concept?  I will probably do that anyway for my project, to avoid the hassle of runtime recompilation of the optimizer.

messages.subject: Multivariate Tobit
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate Tobit
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been banging my head against the wall trying to figure out how to extend a Tobit regression in Stan to the multivariate case. I noticed Dr. Goodrich recently pushed a multivariate Probit model to the example models repo and wondered whether someone might have the time to explain the logic behind it. For the life of me, I cannot see how incrementing 'prev' by rows of the Cholesky factor provides a truncated MVN. (That said, Jacobian adjustment is still an enigma so this is not surprising)

I've attached a data simulation and my attempted model (incrementing the log prob with marginal normals) but it does not properly recover the covariance or correlation structures. For reference, section 3 of Pakman et. al, 2013 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1208.4118.pdf) has the likelihoods for multivariate Probit and Tobit models.

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers,
Andrew

P.S. the latest Cholesky factor optimisations are amazing!

messages.subject_clean: rstan and rstanarm (with major bug fixed) 2.15.x released
messages.body_plain:
We released rstan 2.15.1 a while back, but very little changed

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/NEWS

relative to the 2.14.2 release. However, there were a lot of internal changes in Stan(Headers) for 2.15.0.

We also released rstanarm 2.15.3, which fixed a major bug that was introduced back in January with the 2.14.1 release where models of the form

stan_glmer(y ~ ... + (1 | group1) + (1 | group2), family = binomial())

would produce WRONG RESULTS. This only applies to Bernoulli models with multiple group-specific intercept shifts and no group-specific deviations in the coefficients. If you have estimated any such models in 2017 with rstanarm, you should re-estimate them. The other changes to rstanarm were minor

https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/NEWS

If you are using OSX, it may be necessary to install rstanarm and / or rstan from source to work around the "c++ exception (unknown reason)" error that there are several inconclusive threads about.

Ben

messages.subject: Posterior predictive check for sequential binary outcomes
messages.subject_clean: Posterior predictive check for sequential binary outcomes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question about performing posterior predictive checks for binary responses. I am trying to fit a hierarchical model to choice behavior of human subjects and I am first testing parameter recovery using simulated data. Basically, I simulate N subjects, each of which produces a sequence of binary choices {y1, y2....yt} based on my model. These choices are not independent, since each choice depends on model values calculated based on previous choices.

I understand that posterior predictive check is a recommended way to assess parameter recovery. However, I am not sure how to do this with sequential binary outcomes as observed data; for example, how to generate 50% posterior intervals and check that 50% of the binary outcomes fall into these posterior intervals? Or is there some other way to perform PPC for this type of model?

I would greatly appreciate any comments or suggestions. Thanks!

Best,
Wanting

messages.subject: Jacobians, CDFs, inverse CDFs, and PDFs
messages.subject_clean: Jacobians, CDFs, inverse CDFs, and PDFs
messages.body_plain:
Everyone's always saying they find Jacobians hard.  It really really
helped me to work through a few examples.  This one's very generic
and has the side effect of reinforcing the definition of a density
as the derivative of the cdf.

Suppose

  Y ~ uniform(0, 1)

and you map that to

  Z = normal_inverse_cdf(Y)

assuming that's the inverse of a standard normal (i.e., normal(0, 1))
cumulative density function.  Now you can do that in R:  draw a bunch of Y,
apply the normal inverse CDF, plot the result as a histogram.  It
should look like a standard normal, not like a uniform.  The Jacobian
is what lets us calculate that density.

How do we calculate the density of Z?  We apply the inverse
map back to Y, then multiply by the absolute Jacobian of that
inverse map, which is just the absolute derivative in one dimension.

The inverse of normal_inverse_cdf is just normal_cdf, so everything
cancels neatly:

p_Z(z) = p_Y(std_normal_cdf(z)) * d/dz | std_normal_cdf(z) |

       = 1 * normal(z)

which is just what you want.

It works in general for any continuous CDF because the derivative
of a CDF is just the PDF.  Really the CDFs are much more primitive---they're
what relate to probabilities.  Densities just give you something
convenient to integrate to get back to probaiblities.

Too bad we don't have the inverse CDFs in Stan.  Maybe after
we add a root finder ...

- Bob

P.S.  It's even easier with the standard logistic, because the inverse
      cdf is just inverse logit, or 1 / (1 + exp(-u)).  Differentiating
      that is where the logistic pdf comes from.

messages.body_plain:
Given a basis a 3D tensor is just a 3D array, so the we can specify
it with the N^{3} elements A_{ijk}.  Then the specific operation
implied by the subjectline would be something like

C_{ij} = sum{m, n, o = 1}^{N} A_{imn} B_{jmn}

although you have to be careful about the order if the tensors are
not symmetric.

Without an efficient tensor library in Stan, however, there’s really
nothing to be gained by trying to pack a problem into tensors and
then hack tensor operations as opposed to looping over matrix
operations directly.

messages.body_plain:
Howdy Jonathon

My first question is, do you have a reason to believe your means and standard deviations should be linked like this in your model? Because if there isn't some higher level parameter you know about that you want to estimate, I think it'd be better to not code that in (cause you could be forcing a questionable model on your data). Rather, just give every group a mean and a sigma, and then look at the posteriors to figure out if there is a link or not.

My second is, if you estimate the means and variances of each group, you'll probably want to do some sort of hierarchical model so things don't go crazy. Have you seen these examples? There's the 8 schools one in BDA3, or Bob has some baseball examples (https://youtu.be/qQFF4tPgeWI?t=1h33m43s, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/pooling.html).

Ben

Thanks---that answers my question.  And it reduces the original
question to how to implement this most efficiently in Stan.
I think that's just

  matrix[M, N] A[I];
  matrix[M, N] B[J];

  matrix[I, J] C = tensor_product(A, B);

where we define the function

  // C_{ij} = sum{m, n = 1}^{N} A_{imn} B_{jmn}
  matrix tensor_product(matrix[] A matrix[] B) {
    matrix[size(A), size(B)] C;
    for (j in 1:J)
      for (i in 1:I)
        c[i, j] = sum(A[i] .* B[j]);
    return c;
  }

I like when these things work out about as neatly as the original
formula (I removed the o variable as it wasn't used).

We could technically write analytic derivatives for sum(matrix .* matrix)
that would be both faster and less memory intensive than what you get
from the above.  I turned it into an issue because I think the above
is a pain for a user to have to write if this is a common operation:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/543

- Bob

Hi Ben,

Thanks for the suggestion!

In general, I agree that forcing the relationship will not be desirable.  However, I ran into a specific dataset where an exploratory analysis (just plotting group means against group sd's) was highly suggestive of a linear relationship.  So, I decided to play around and see if I could model it.

Creating separate variance components for each group is problematic because the data is highly unbalanced with small sample sizes for many of the groups.  In general I'm happy with complete pooling, but a partial pooling model of the variance component is an interesting idea.  I'll give that a try.

Do you expect that modeling the variance as a linear function of the mean is doomed to cause computational problems?

Thanks,

Jonathon

messages.subject: Wiener Diffusion Model - multiple constrains for the same parameter
messages.subject_clean: Wiener Diffusion Model - multiple constrains for the same parameter
messages.body_plain:
The non-decision time parameter is notoriously difficult to estimate.
The first thing I would do is to remove obvious outlier (fast) RTs.
If you are uncomfortable with a simple cut-off approach, the dmat toolbox (Matlab) has a nifty approach.

Otherwise, people have been advocating to use a mixture model (see eg the HDDM toolbox in Python), such that the likelihood has these two parts:
- the wiener pdf
- a uniform that spans all possible Date

Let's say you fix your mixture to 95% wiener and 5% uniform.
Then, in pseudo code

target += log(.05*exp(uniform_lpdf(y|alpha, beta)) + .95*exp(wiener_lpdf(y|alpha_w,tau_w,beta_w,delta_w))

Or using log_sum_exp

log05 = log(.05)
log95 = log(.05)
target += log_sum_exp(log05 + uniform_lpdf(y|alpha, beta), log95 + wiener_lpdf(y|alpha_w,tau_w,beta_w,delta_w)

Let me know if this works, I haven't been able to test this.

Guido

I'm not super familiar with modeling this, so maybe someone else can jump in. This sounds like something someone would have experience with.

Probly the easiest way to diagnose if a model is neurotic is some way (without digging into the math) is to just simulate data from the thing you're trying to fit, and then trying to fit it. Like, it's easy to generate data from a distribution normal(a/b, 1.0), but then trying to estimate 'a' and 'b' separately in a model is going to be hard (cause there are many 'a's and 'b's that are gonna give you good fits).

If Stan fits the simulated data easily, then the issue is probably something about the model not explaining your data very well that's causing your issues.

Hopefully that helps :D

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Bayes posterior mean is _calibrated_:  If we label thata_hat = E(theta|y), then E(theta | theta_hat) = theta_hat, where the expectation is taken over the joint distribution of y and theta.

But Bayes posterior mean is not _unbiased_.  Unbiased is E(theta_hat | theta) = theta.  Bayes posterior mean can never be unbiased under this definition.

Unbiasedness is an important principle in _measurement_, not so much in _estimation_.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior predictive check for sequential binary outcomes
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Posterior predictive check for sequential binary outcomes
messages.body_plain:
The sequential nature of the data isn't a problem, but we're
usually estimating continuous parameters with Stan.  You can
use any kind of posterior statistic you want to do posterior
p-value checks, such as aggregated counts of subsequences.  I
just did a quick overview of the Cook et al. method:

http://andrewgelman.com/2017/04/12/bayesian-posteriors-calibrated/

We need to put a lot more of this stuff in the manual.  And
you can certainly do the kind of visual diagnostics that Gelman
et al. recommend in Bayesian Data Analysis.

- Bob

> On May 1, 2017, at 12:30 AM, John Jumper <john.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> To be fair, I am not planning to use NUTS on the neural network parameters themselves.  I have a trained variational autoencoder (a la Kingma and Welling https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114) using PyTorch to handle the deep learning model.  The parameters on which I will do HMC are the latent dimensions of the autoencoder.  I expect that this space should be clean enough by construction of the autoencoder, otherwise the gaussian variational posterior would not achieve a good entropy bound.  In the worst case, I might need parallel tempering (which I assume Stan doesn't have).

Nope, no parallel tempering.

> It would be really nice if Stan's MCMC engine were split out into a proper library that could be used outside of Stan.  Please correct me if I am wrong, but is it as simple as writing a virtual base class that implements the Model concept?  I will probably do that anyway for my project, to avoid the hassle of runtime recompilation of the optimizer.

That'd be the least invasive way to do it.  There's a lot of functionality in
those methods that depend on our constraining and unconstraining
transforms and the blocks in a Stan program.  And it's probably
assuming you have a templated log_prob function that gets autodiffed to
form a gradient.  It used to have a log_prob_grad function that rolled
them together.

One of the things we need to do for Stan 3 is rethink that model
class.  So we'll probably be doing this ourselves over the next year
or two.

A better approach would probably be to more cleanly abstract the
algorithms.  That's never been a huge concern for us because we only
have one language.  Implementing NUTS is relatively easy (though it's
subtle and there are a lot of pitfalls---I just meant in terms of
amount of code).  It's all the derivatives and tie-ins to the language
that are hard.

If you can figure out how to refactor the MCMC lib into a standalone library
that doesn't depend on our model concept that we can use elsewhere, that'd be
great.  When Alp and Dustin built ADVI, they wound up writing their own
optimizer because the L-BFGS built into Stan is also tied up with our model class.
So it'd be useful to us internally, too.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Identifying causes of divergences
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I was hoping you could help me with a question about divergences.

My understanding (from the "Brief Guide to Stan's Warnings" and the manual's section on "Diagnosing and Eliminating Divergences") is that, when divergences occur, experienced HMC operators can often figure out which parameters are to blame from model diagnostics and "pairs" plots. My question is, what are we looking for?

Do we just look for funnel shapes, or is there more? Do the XY coordinates of the red points in the pairs plot tell us anything? If the number of parameters is large (and the number of parameter pairs is even larger), are there ways to narrow down the search space?

Sorry if this is written down somewhere and I just missed it!

Thanks in advance,

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Michael, thanks for sending me your exploration of divergence, it was very interesting.

Unfortunately, I'm still having a lot of trouble achieving convergence.  I tried specifying half-Cauchy(0,1) distributions and multiplying by cScale in the model.  Even with adapt_delta at .99 there were hundreds of divergent transitions. I then tried switching from half-Cauchy distributions to half-Normals.  This actually made things worse in terms of rhat and ess.

So, I started to suspect that the problem might go beyond the geometry of the log-likelihood.  It turns out that the model with no pooling on the variance components also fails to converge.  Presumably, this is because many of the groups have only 1 or 2 data points making it impossible to estimate individual standard deviations.  In these cases I'm happy for the prior variance to be used, but maybe the difference in the scale of the prior is causing convergence problems?

My current plan is to get the model with no pooling working before trying the hierarchical model again.  I'm hoping this can be done with the right selection of informative priors, but I'd be happy to hear any suggestions.

Thanks again,

Jonathon

messages.subject: Re: Gaussian variance as a linear function of the mean

messages.body_plain:
Jonathon,

in your earlier post you use fabs:

 lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  fabs(beta[bioID[i]]) + sigma)

I first about using the log-likelihood of the normal distribution direct to used
a squared version, instead take the absolut.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution#Maximum_entropy

The mean parameter remains the same, your sigma has to be squared, eg. the variance.
You would avoid the fabs. Also the variances of the normal can be added,
in your example you added the parameter interpreted as SD. At least I would square and add
them and then take the sqrt.

 lr[i] ~ normal(beta[bioID[i]] ,  sqrt(square(beta[bioID[i]]) + square(sigma)))

A problem might be also the multi-modality, eg. square(sigma) and square(-sigma) leading to same.
Thus I think the constraint on sigma remain necessary. But what about square(beta[bioID[i]]))?

Andre

messages.subject: Issues with ODE solving.
messages.subject_clean: Issues with ODE solving.
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

This is my first post on the M.L. so thanks for adding me to it. I've
stumbled upon stan last week and I've been trying to use it in a project
we have in my team, whose goal is to compute the entropy of posterior
distributions to do optimal experiment design in biology. Should it be
of interest to you, our team is a joint research group between Inria and
the Institut Pasteur, and our offices are located on the latter's campus
in Paris.

The model I am currently working on is a simplistic representation of a
gene circuit known as the toggle switch. The data we have is a time
series of the behavior of the two proteins of interest of our system,
and in a first time, we want to compute the posterior distributions of
its four parameters. This requires that we solve the differential
equations of the system to get the theoretic behavior for the parameters
and then compute their likelihood. This is highly similar to the problem
presented in figure 19.4 of the reference manual.

Unfortunately, I can't figure out how to get the equation solving part
to work. As of know, shall I run the attached code on the attached data,
stan constantly fails with

100 times
> Rejecting initial value:
>  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

then:

> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
> Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values,
> or reparameterizing the model.
> Initialization failed.

I've also attached the complete output.

I've tried removing part of the code to see which one has to blame and

messages.subject: Re: Identifying causes of divergences
messages.subject_clean: Identifying causes of divergences
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm sure the developers have better answers for you, but here is two general steps I might use:
- Build models from something simple (that works), and add complexity. Chances are you will identify the step where the added complexity gives you problems, and you can from there think of ways to overcome the divergences.
- Along a similar vein is to estimate your full model, but using tight priors - maybe even "unreasonably" tight - and then slacken them one at the time. E.g. you might find that estimated covariance matrices give you divergences with too uninformative priors.

Finally, make sure you use the recommended functions and transformations as opposed to writing things yourself (example: not ln( theta*exp(l1) + (1-theta)exp(l2)). Use the built in log_mix(theta, lp1,lp2).

best,
Ole-Petter

Hi, Ben

On Wednesday, April 26, 2017 at 1:09:23 AM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, April 26, 2017 at 12:57:23 AM UTC-4, Paul Johnson wrote:
> > I'm not an Rstan user.
>
> Yet.
>
> > Can one of you point me at code for an Rstan job that runs for a day or so and tests out a lot of the bells and whistles? One that does not crash at the end would be an extra good choice :)
>
> I don't think I have any interesting examples of long-running code that I can share, but we have definitely seen Stan run for days and come out fine in the end. You could try a simple Stan program without data like
>
> transformed data {
>   int K = 5000; // or other large integer
> }
> parameters {
>   corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
> }
> model {}
>
> > The student who I've assigned to test this out has a Rstan job that takes 8 hours on her MS Windows computer, where it runs fine (I'm told, at least), but when she puts that in the cluster, it runs for about 22 hours and then has a crash that looks suspiciously like a g++ memory allocation error, which I paste in below.
>
> That looks to me like either:
> the Stan program got compiled on a worker node and when the stanfit object was passed back to the analysis node, the worker node shut down leaving a dangling pointer to the stanmodel object inside the stanfit object
> an overly aggressive server script decided to delete the shared object in tempdir() because it wasn't touched for a certain number of hours
>
> I think the first is more likely. The solution to that would involve compiling the thing on the analysis node with stan_model() and passing the resulting object to the worker nodes when you call sampling(). Server setups vary, but I know people have done Stan stuff on the Columbia clusters which also use torque.
>

I got to the bottom of this problem. The submission script did not have "--vanilla" in the R program call.  I always do that, as a matter of habit, because it eliminates usage of saved workspaces (.RData) or user profile and such. The student omitted that, and when we put it in, then the job stopped crashing.

Can a reasonable explanation be like this? The student used Rstan on a Windows system using the standard Rtools setup, which has older gcc than we have in the cluster.  This left behind .RData and an old session traveled to the cluster, where the special Windows magic was not compatible with the RHEL 6, gcc-6.3 version of Rstan. When R started, and loaded that workspace, there were some Windows-build rstan objects floating about.

I don't have access to carefully inspect the user's account, but it is also possible there is something untoward in .Rprofile.  I'm trying to find out.

It is a one node only, multiple core model.  No MPI issues are tied in.  I need to work out the MPI version next, because the multicore code takes about 1 day per MCMC chain, and the project is supposed to explore 1000s of these things.  I will post separate questions to get help on that.

This left me wondering about the Rstan customization of the Makevars file, how that is affected by "--vanilla".
> Ben

> So if I understand your model correctly, each set of data you model as a Gaussian process with different means but the same covariance.
>
> So:
> for (d in 1:D)
>     y[d] ~ multi_normal(mu[d], H);

> Where 'd' are your days, and H is the small covariance matrix (the same H as in your model, not the covariance matrix for all D days lumped together).
>
> Can't you just write your model like this? There is the issue that at each day you need to have data measured at the same points for them to share the covariance matrix, but if you have that, then you can get the speedup you're looking for by doing:
>
> L = cholesky_decomposition(H)
> for (d in 1:D)
>     y[d] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu[d], L);
>
> It's a Cholesky instead of an inversion cause computing matrix inverses by themselves is a Bad Idea. Solving Ax = b is strongly preferred over trying to compute A^-1 and then multiplying it by b. messages.body_plain:
I recently updated my R and RStan installations in Windows 10, and it broke RStan. I was previously using R 3.3.3 and RStan 2.14.2. When I updated, suddenly R would crash when I tried to run models that ran perfectly before. I tried uninstalling all versions of R, Rtools, and all R libraries, and reinstalling from scratch, but to no avail.

To be precise, this is what I've tried installing:
R 3.4
Rtools 3.4 (most recent version, notably non-frozen)
RStan 15.1

A minimal example of the problem in in the attached .stan and .R files. Basically, R crashes when you call stan() on a previously compiled model with a vector parameter with a dimension larger than 43, but only when you call stan() for the second time on that model. Stan compiles the model find and will sample from it as long as sampling is part of the same stan() call as compilation. But if I try to sample from a previously compiled model, R crashes. Interestingly, I have some saved Stan models compiled in my previous R/Rstan install (Stan 2.14.2 in R 3.3.3 with I believe Rtools 3.3). Saved in the sense that I called > save(fit, file = "fit.RData") in R, modulo the file/object names. If I load one of them into R 3.4 and use RStan 15.1 to sample from that model, I have zero problems.

Note: when R crashes, it gives the error code 255, though occasionally it will give the code 5.

Everything seems to work perfectly in Ubuntu with a fresh install of R 3.4 and RStan 15.1, so I suspect it has something to do with Rtools and the compiler it makes available.

Other things I've tried in Windows:

1) Install RStan 15.1 in R 3.3.3 using Rtools 3.3. This caused R to crash when the first time stan() was called on the model, though notably after compilation.
2) Install RStan 15.1 in R 3.4 using Rtools 3.4 from source. This threw an error - it had trouble installing RcppEigen for some reason (I don't have the error message recorded anywhere, sorry, but I believe it complained about the c++ compiler).

So I have two questions: 1) Is there a tweak to the installation process that will make everything work? Or, failing that, 2) How do I install an old version of RStan so I can get back to work?

Thanks,
Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying causes of divergences
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Identifying causes of divergences
messages.body_plain:
You're looking for where the divergences happen.  Are
they in the neck of a funnel?  Are you getting a banana-shaped
posterior (multiplicative non-identifiability) or long narrow
ridges (additive non-identifiability).   Are all the errors showing
up on a boundary of parameter space?

What you're looking for ideally is a posterior that is independent
standard normal in every dimension.   Reparameterization can help with
independence and standardization can help with the scaling.

And I'll second Ole Petter Hansen's general advice on starting
simple and building up.  You can use our built-ins, which sometimes
give you more arithmetic stability---sometimes the cause is
floating-point arithmetic, not the model itself per se.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: g++ profiling on sampling function?
messages.body_plain:
I'm doing tech support on one of the student projects. I'm looking for a command line/Unix user who can point me in the right direction. I want to know how to profile Stan's internal activities, the C++ side calculations.

A user here wants to run 1000s of variants of an MCMC rstan project. On the compute cluster, for some not-yet-solved-reason, the completion of a chain with 10000 iterations requires 24 hours (but it takes 12 hours on my RedHat Linux workstations).  We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping.  The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program.

Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?

I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line.  As in all programming manuals, I  understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model.  Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do.   I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.

I've not done this in a while, but I'm pretty sure I'd need to rebuild Stan itself with profiling and debugging symbols. After that, I have some experience in other C and Objective-C projects, but not in C++.

Paul Johnson

messages.subject: Re: g++ profiling on sampling function?
messages.subject_clean: g++ profiling on sampling function?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

On Friday, May 5, 2017 at 12:21:04 AM UTC-4, Paul Johnson wrote:
> Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?

One can download or git clone CmdStan from

https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/

and execute

make stan-update
make -j8 build
echo "CFLAGS += -pg" >> make/local
make /path/to/stanfile/without/dotstan/extension

Followed by

cd /path/to/directory/with/stanfile
./executable_name sample data file = my.data.R

where the my.data.R file has to be created from R using rstan::rstan::stan_rdump() . And then do the usual gprof stuff.

However, when you do all that, you will find that almost all of the time is spent evaluating the gradient, which is not that useful unless you are prepared to write C++ functions that substitute analytical gradient calculations for Stan's autodiff. Maybe it comes to that, but usually the place to start is with the model and the geometry of the posterior distribution it implies. By default Stan does up to 2^10 - 1 gradient evaluations per MCMC iteration, but will do fewer if it hits the U-turn point on each MCMC iteration before doing 10 leapfrog steps. So, if you can go from 9 leapfrog steps to 6 with various reparameterizations, then it will take much less time to run.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question re regression with noisy observation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question re regression with noisy observation
messages.body_plain:
You want to turn this around and ask yourself how the data
comes about.  I think what you're saying is that you
have an independent model for some underlying x, and
then instead of modeling y based on x, you model change in
y based on change in x.

There's nothing wrong with that model per se, but it's unusual.
And it doesn't give you a model of the first y.  A more
common approach to doing this is to take a moving average type
time series model, where

  x[n + 1] ~ normal(x[n] | mu, sigma);

  y[n + 1] ~ normal(y[n + 1] | phi, tau);

To answer your direct question, what you want to do is non-center
this bit:

  x ~ normal (x_mu, x_sigma);

replacing it with

  x_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

  x = x_mu + x_raw * x_sigma;

- Bob

I would choose a skewed t-distribution, the skewness parameter to be positive with low degree of freedom
and another student-t and having a mixture distribution together with an mixture parameter for each bioID.

Added:

This fits your group mean:

qqplot(tapply(lr,bioID,mean),rnorm(10000,0,0.5))

and skewed t-distribution fits your errors:

lrN <- lr-tapply(lr,bioID,mean)[bioID]
fit<-gamlss(lrN ~ 1,family=ST5())
qqplot(lrN,rST5(1000,-.0712,exp(-0.97),0.007,exp(0.28)))

Then we have:

means ~ normal(0, 0.5);
lr ~ ST5(means[bioID] -.0712,exp(-0.97),0.007,exp(0.28));

The ST5 is the skewed t-dist. from this forum.

Andre

messages.body_plain:
Hey Arthur

I had a look at your model. I think the issue is that the first 't' in your list of times should be greater than the initial time, t0. I made this modification to your model and it started sampling for me.

In your data you have ts[1] == 0 as well as t0 == 0. ts[1] needs to be greater than t0.

The lack of error messages is a problem some other folks have fun into recently. There's something where if an error gets thrown in initialization it's not being reported back (Stan should have been able to tell you about the t[1] > t0 thing itself). I think it's being worked on right now (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2294)

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> On May 5, 2017, at 12:21 AM, Paul Johnson <paulj...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I'm doing tech support on one of the student projects. I'm looking for a command line/Unix user who can point me in the right direction. I want to know how to profile Stan's internal activities, the C++ side calculations.
>
> A user here wants to run 1000s of variants of an MCMC rstan project. On the compute cluster, for some not-yet-solved-reason, the completion of a chain with 10000 iterations requires 24 hours (but it takes 12 hours on my RedHat Linux workstations).  We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping.  The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program.

Your best bet is to have the student send us the program so we can help optimize it.

> Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?
>
> I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line.  As in all programming manuals, I  understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model.  Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do.   I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.

So have we all.  We're always happy to take performance improvement pull requests if you can find a problem.

I should warn you up front that our code is very tightly dependent on our low-level memory allocation and inlining at optimization level -O3.   Profiling at -O0, etc. won't help, and when you run at -O3 so much is inlined that it's hard to see down into the lower-level code.  You can also run into bias issues where simple instrumentation of the code provides very different answers than profiling.

Any help here would be appreciated, too.

> I've not done this in a while, but I'm pretty sure I'd need to rebuild Stan itself with profiling and debugging symbols. After that, I have some experience in other C and Objective-C projects, but not in C++.

You may find the C++ a bit daunting in Stan---it's heavily templated with a ton of metaprogramming.  But as Ben says, what we see under profiling is that almost all the time's spent in computing the backward pass of automatic differentiation for gradients.  It's effectively interpreted code for computing the chain rule.

- Bob

> initialization it's not being reported back (Stan should have been able
> to tell you about the t[1] > t0 thing itself). I think it's being worked
> on right now (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2294)
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi, all,

I'm the student in question, and I've attached my code here. I've already tried to done some code optimization on my own using the manual; however, I have no experience in C++, so there are probably further improvements that can be made.

Most perplexing to me is the difference in run time across systems. It takes Paul 12 hours on his RedHat workstations, and I've clocked it at 10-12 hours on my Windows workstation. The fact that it takes twice as long to run on the cluster is baffling!

Thanks in advance for your help!
Jennifer

On Sunday, May 7, 2017 at 12:21:11 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On May 5, 2017, at 12:21 AM, Paul Johnson <paulj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm doing tech support on one of the student projects. I'm looking for a command line/Unix user who can point me in the right direction. I want to know how to profile Stan's internal activities, the C++ side calculations.
> >
> > A user here wants to run 1000s of variants of an MCMC rstan project. On the compute cluster, for some not-yet-solved-reason, the completion of a chain with 10000 iterations requires 24 hours (but it takes 12 hours on my RedHat Linux workstations).  We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping.  The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program.
>
> Your best bet is to have the student send us the program so we can help optimize it.
>
>
> > Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?
> >
> > I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line.  As in all programming manuals, I  understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model.  Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do.   I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.
>
> So have we all.  We're always happy to take performance improvement pull requests if you can find a problem.
>
> I should warn you up front that our code is very tightly dependent on our low-level memory allocation and inlining at optimization level -O3.   Profiling at -O0, etc. won't help, and when you run at -O3 so much is inlined that it's hard to see down into the lower-level code.  You can also run into bias issues where simple instrumentation of the code provides very different answers than profiling.
>

messages.subject: learning stab: what? how?
messages.subject_clean: learning stab: what? how?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I discovered Stan less than one year ago, almost at the same time as bayesian statistics, using Richard Mcelreath 'Statistical Rethinking'  and for last few months I have it to my work routine. In this thread, I would like to ask for some advice or someone who would share his or her experience on what should be the best way to learn it beyond a superficial level. Any tips or ideas would be welcome.

My main problem is that I am somehow trapped between easy problems, for which I don't need to use Stan, and difficult ones, that are too often too difficult- I guess this applies to most 'deeper level' languages. Most of my workflow are easy problems and for these, I use standard R packages, since these are much faster for exploratory analysis. Although I try to use stan as much as possible, it is just not practical given my time constraints.

I am only driven to use Stan whenever I need more flexibility than it is provided by standard packages -typically hierarchical models that I need to customize for my purposes. Then the obstacle I face is a massive learning curve on many fronts: modeling, computational, etc,... : is my specification wrong? is my code inefficient? Am I trying to do something that just can't be done (maybe that's why there no ready to use package for it)? When I face these challenges, I feel I do not understand well enough what the software is doing for me. I typically plunge in the manual or forums.  These resources are great (the manual really is!), but massive. Too often, I end up giving up.

Does anyone have any suggestion on how to learn the language and what lies behind it in a more or less practical and systematic way? Is it worth, for instance, to spend some time reading about MCMC simulation techniques (some time in my bayesian course I learns Gibbs,Metropolis and had a sense of HMC)? Is it worth to read about data structures and language specific functions, for instance?

Anyway, I am just looking for you folks to share your experience with me.

messages.body_plain:
1.  I recommend rstanarm for the easy problems.  rstanarm has lots of functionality that regular regression software doesn't have, including draws from posterior, informative priors, regularization, and splines.

2.  To get into other uses, you can look at the example models and the case studies at the documentation on the Stan webpage.

3.  I recommend you focus on modeling and simulation of predictions, not on MCMC.  Stan does the MCMC for you.  At some point, to become a power-user it is helpful to understand Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, but this should not be your first priority.

A

El martes, 9 de mayo de 2017, 23:30:40 (UTC-4), Michael Betancourt escribió:
> But if you _did_ want to learn more about MCMC and HMC

> > 1.  I recommend rstanarm for the easy problems.  rstanarm has lots of functionality that regular regression software doesn't have, including draws from posterior, informative priors, regularization, and splines.
> >
> > 2.  To get into other uses, you can look at the example models and the case studies at the documentation on the Stan webpage.
> >
> > 3.  I recommend you focus on modeling and simulation of predictions, not on MCMC.  Stan does the MCMC for you.  At some point, to become a power-user it is helpful to understand Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, but this should not be your first priority.
> >
> > A
> >
> > > On May 9, 2017, at 7:39 PM, Luis G <luism....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > I discovered Stan less than one year ago, almost at the same time as bayesian statistics, using Richard Mcelreath 'Statistical Rethinking'  and for last few months I have it to my work routine. In this thread, I would like to ask for some advice or someone who would share his or her experience on what should be the best way to learn it beyond a superficial level. Any tips or ideas would be welcome.

> > > My main problem is that I am somehow trapped between easy problems, for which I don't need to use Stan, and difficult ones, that are too often too difficult- I guess this applies to most 'deeper level' languages. Although I try to use stan as much as possible, it is just not practical given my time constraints.
> > >
> > > I am only driven to use Stan whenever I need more flexibility than it is provided by standard packages -typically hierarchical models that I need to customize for my purposes. Then the obstacle I face is a massive learning curve on many fronts: modeling, computational, etc,... : is my specification wrong? is my code inefficient? Am I trying to do something that just can't be done (maybe that's why there no ready to use package for it)? When I face these challenges, I feel I do not understand well enough what the software is doing for me. I typically plunge in the manual or forums. messages.body_plain:
> On May 10, 2017, at 10:38 AM, Mohammed Effat <mbef...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
> I want to double check two things:
> 1) the model block in stan is for inputting the prior and likelihood models, not the posterior pdf. correct?

Stan specifies a density up to a constant---it doesn't even have
to be a Bayesian posterior.  If you code the log likelihood plus
log prior, that's equal to the log posterior up to an additive
constant.  So there's no difference.

> 2) the examples given in stan user guide all involve the use of standard distributions for the models. You need to define the log density up to an additive constant.
Multiplying two Gaussians would require normalization.  If you
write the density down, we can help.

- Bob

Multi-indexing matrices works just like in R.  The key to understanding it is that
if you have this:

  matrix[M, N] a;

  int<lower=1, upper=M> rs[I];
  int<lower=1, upper=N> cs[J];

then the way a[rs, cs] is defined produces an I x J matrix
whose entries are defined as

  a[rs, cs][i, j] = a[rs[i], cs[j]]

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical Bayesian model and constrained optimization in RStan?! Modeling
messages.body_plain:
> On May 9, 2017, at 3:34 AM, Mohammed Effat <mbef...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
> I have a complex pdf based on hierarchical Bayesian formalism where x depends on the hyperpriors w' and w'' as w=Gamma(beta/2,2/zeta)

??? w' and w'' don't show up in this expression.  Can you write out
what your density is or how to define a random variable with that
distribution?

> where Gamma is the gamma distribution with parameters beta and zeta. The resulting negative log likelihood for joint posterior pdf is in the attached picture. I want to sample both of w', w'', and x. My approach is to use the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler. I have the following questions below:
>
> 1) I thought before that I can split the sampling process that, I sample w' and w'' from the gamma distribution first.

No.  Stan doesn't split anything.  You want to do everything jointly.  All you
need to do is give it a continuously differentiable log density with parameters defined
with appropriate constraints.

> And as they become known values, they can be taken out from the exponential as normalizing constants leaving only x to be sampled. As I have the constraint x>=0, this makes the posterior truncated mulitivariate Gaussian. Consequently, I thought of sampling x using the exact algorithm by Pakman and Paninski. Is this approach feasible?
>
> 2) I want to use the HMC algorithm by Stan, however I want to know if the optimizer in Stan to estimate the MAP supports the x>=0 constraint or it is for x>0 only?

Don't use MAP if you can fit a Bayesian estimate unless someone's making you do it because they don't like Bayes.

>
> 3) Can you refer me to a good RStan example to train myself who to sample a complex hierarchical posteriors like the one attached?

Most of our examples are of that form. Check out the case studies
on the web.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] g++ profiling on sampling function?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] g++ profiling on sampling function?
messages.body_plain:
The usual suspects for cluster slowdown are:

  * high latency file I/O

  * limited memory

  * memory/CPU contention from shared jobs

We haven't paid a lot of attention to any of these issues,
I'm afraid, so any improvements to the base code for these
situations would be appreciated.

If you send us your Stan code, we can help optimize.

This list is shutting down, so if you wouldn't mind, please
take this up again here in a new thread:

http://discourse.mc-stan.org

- Bob

> On May 9, 2017, at 9:52 AM, jbru...@gmail.com wrote:
>
>
> Hi, all,
>
> I'm the student in question, and I've attached my code here. I've already tried to done some code optimization on my own using the manual; however, I have no experience in C++, so there are probably further improvements that can be made.
>
> Most perplexing to me is the difference in run time across systems. It takes Paul 12 hours on his RedHat workstations, and I've clocked it at 10-12 hours on my Windows workstation. The fact that it takes twice as long to run on the cluster is baffling!
>
> Thanks in advance for your help!
> Jennifer
>
> On Sunday, May 7, 2017 at 12:21:11 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On May 5, 2017, at 12:21 AM, Paul Johnson <paulj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm doing tech support on one of the student projects. I'm looking for a command line/Unix user who can point me in the right direction. I want to know how to profile Stan's internal activities, the C++ side calculations.
> >
> > A user here wants to run 1000s of variants of an MCMC rstan project. On the compute cluster, for some not-yet-solved-reason, the completion of a chain with 10000 iterations requires 24 hours (but it takes 12 hours on my RedHat Linux workstations).  We have ruled out the usual sources of slowdown, such as disk writes or memory swapping.  The R profile seems to indicate that almost all of the time is spent in the Rstan "sampling" function. I started to wonder what I can do to quantify the limitations on the program.
>
> Your best bet is to have the student send us the program so we can help optimize it.
>
>
> > Can I find somebody who runs the command line Stan who can tell me if it is possible to run g++ in profiling mode?
> >
> > I've been reading the Stan programming manual and I gather there is a way to compile a stan project to run from the command line.  As in all programming manuals, I  understand that there are many "dos and don'ts" for writing a fast model.  Without becoming a Stan expert, recognizing certain "bad tendencies" in user code, its not clear what I ought to do.   I'd really like to have a profile. Over the years, I've had plenty of examples where the profiler points at slow spots that you would never guess.
>
> So have we all.  We're always happy to take performance improvement pull requests if you can find a problem.
>
> I should warn you up front that our code is very tightly dependent on our low-level memory allocation and inlining at optimization level -O3.   Profiling at -O0, etc. won't help, and when you run at -O3 so much is inlined that it's hard to see down into the lower-level code.  You can also run into bias issues where simple instrumentation of the code provides very different answers than profiling.
>
> Any help here would be appreciated, too.
>
> > I've not done this in a while, but I'm pretty sure I'd need to rebuild Stan itself with profiling and debugging symbols. After that, I have some experience in other C and Objective-C projects, but not in C++.
>
> You may find the C++ a bit daunting in Stan---it's heavily templated with a ton of metaprogramming.  But as Ben says, what we see under profiling is that almost all the time's spent in computing the backward pass of automatic differentiation for gradients.  It's effectively interpreted code for computing the chain rule.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Converting a logit to a probit model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Converting a logit to a probit model
messages.body_plain:
> On May 10, 2017, at 10:57 AM, new2...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I first have a basic question and then a perhaps trickier question. First, I have set up a basic two-level logistic regression model in STAN, and that works fine. But a co-author is asking for the probit formulation instead. I have looked in the manual and I see that it shouldn't be too hard to make the switch, but I'm having trouble because it seems that the probit (Phi) is introduced as part of the likelihood function (see below) whereas I've been using binomial_logit after the for loop:
>
> y[n] ~ bernoulli(Phi(alpha + beta * x[n]));
>
> How should I go about redoing this as a probit?

Is that a trick question?  It's already a probit.  Probit just means
using Phi rather than inv_logit as the (inverse) link function.

> The second question is that we will be using WAIC to compare models with different covariates, so I calculated the deviance for each observation with the binomial_logit_lpmf probability mass function. I cannot discern if there is a comparable way to do this for probit models.

No difference at all.  Literally the only difference is using inv_logit vs. Phi.
We also have a Phi_approx that's almost as efficient as inv_logit, but on the
scale of Phi.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, May 9, 2017 at 9:52:09 AM UTC-4, jbru...@gmail.com wrote:
> Most perplexing to me is the difference in run time across systems. It takes Paul 12 hours on his RedHat workstations, and I've clocked it at 10-12 hours on my Windows workstation. The fact that it takes twice as long to run on the cluster is baffling!

I would guess that the cluster nodes are not picking up the CXXFLAGS in your ~/.R/Makevars file. If you call stan_model() with verbose = TRUE, you can see the compiler output in the logs to see what optimization level it used.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to go around "Rejecting initial value"?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to go around "Rejecting initial value"?
messages.body_plain:
You get rejection when the random inits don't have support in
the model.  That's usually because there are missing constraints
in parameter declarations or illegal math or missing definitions.

I'd recommend starting simpler and building up to a more complex
model.

The syntax is now

  target += lp;

rather than

  increment_log_prob(lp);

- Bob

> > >
> > > Hey Stan Group,
> > > I am new to Bayes and try to apply it in the next month to some hidden Markov model inference for proteins. Sofar my toy triexponential decay model does not behave well.
> > >  R_hat goes to inifity even though my Priors are to my understanding really restrictive what am I doing wrong here? The rates are seperated by an order of Magnitude. So they should be distinguishabel...
> > >
> > > regress_code_simple = """
> > > data {
> > >  int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
> > >  real counts[N]; // response variable
> > >  real time[N]; // predictor variable
> > > }
> > > parameters {
> > >  real<lower=0> rate1;
> > >  real<lower=rate1> rate2;
> > >  real<lower=rate2> rate3;
> >
> > Easier to just do
> >
> >   positive_ordered[3] rate;
> >
> > >  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation
> > > }
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >  real mu[N]; // fitted values
> > > for(i in 1:N)
> > >  mu[i] = 0.4*exp(-rate1*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate2*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate3*time[i]);
> >
> > This can be vectorized as follows:
> >
> >   mu = 0.4 * exp(-rate1 * time)
> >      + 0.3 * exp(-rate2 * time)
> >      + 0.3 * exp(-rate3 * time));
> >
> > if you declare time as a vector:
> >
> >   vector[N] time;
> >
> > But the bigger problem is that it's not going to be identified because
> > you've introduced essentially three regression-like coefficient based
> > on the same coefficient and you've given the first two rates plenty of
> > latitude.
> >
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >  real alpha;
> > >  real beta;
> > >  alpha = 1.0;
> > >  beta  = 1.0;
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >  sigma ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
> >
> > Much better to just do
> >
> >   sigma ~ gamma(1, 1);
> >
> > >
> > >  rate1 ~ normal(0,5)T[0,];
> > >  rate2 ~ normal(9,5)T[0,];
> > >  rate3 ~ normal(95,10)T[0,];
> >
> > This isn't the right truncations to normalize:
> >

> >   rate[2] ~ normal(9, 5) T[rate[1], 0];
> >   rate[3] ~ normal(95, 10) T[rate[2], 0];
> >
> > You can drop the first truncation for efficiency, but you need
> > the next two because they depend on parameters.
> >
> > >  counts ~ normal(mu,sigma);
> >
> > But I have no idea why you'd do this.  If you want to define a mixture,
> > I'd suggest looking at the mixture modeling section of the manual.  You
> > mix the whole distributions, not the means.
> >
> >
> > > }
> > > """
> > > The error analysis is bad at the beginning and then is fine for some time
> >
> > The only parameters that look OK here are the rate and sigma.  You may have
> > numerical issues in the mu leading to underflow and overflow with the exp(),
> > but I'm guessing you really meant to implement a mixture model, not something
> > with an odd composite mean.
> >

messages.body_plain:
First thing to do is test your gamma implementations before
trying to fit.

It helps if you say how things failed.

Rather than log(tgamma(x)), you want lgamma(x).

It should look like this:

  return log(c)
         + c * a * log(b)
         + (c * a - 1) * log(x)
         - (b * x)^c
         - lgamma(a);

then either use the function exposer in RStan or test within the
Stan program to make sure you get the right values using some kind
of independent implementation.

- Bob

> On May 12, 2017, at 9:14 AM, Ghislain d'Entremont <ghislaind...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> Following up on Mike's question from last summer, have we found a 'solution' or reliable hack besides the normality approximation? Interestingly, I only get problems when I add parameters to my model such that the kappa for a given participant/condition is a linear combination of multiple main effect and interaction terms. Might the problem, in my case, be related to that fact the linear combination of parameters going into Kappa, each with uninformative priors, increase the likelihood of kappa being evaluated at the boundaries?
>
> Thanks,
>
> On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 9:32:29 PM UTC-3, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> As has been mentioned before, use of the von_mises(mu,kappa) with largish (>10?) values for the kappa parameter tends to yield the exception:
>
> "Exception thrown at line 80: Error in function boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<double>(double,double): numeric overflow"
>
> Now, the solution thus far is to use the fact the fact that as kappa increases, normal(mu,sqrt(1/kappa)) approximates von_mises(mu,kappa) and throw in an if statement using the former when kappa is, say, >10. However, beyond being a bit of a hack, in some circumstances this can cause considerable slowdown. For example, I use the von_mises for mixture data where individual data points get their own value for kappa (well, there's some repetition/grouping, but that's inconsequential here), so I have to do the if-check for every data point. After playing a bit, it seems that when the true value is close to the value used for the if-check, you get dramatically slower performance compared to a version that just uses the von_mises alone. However, in that case sometimes a chain will simply fail to initialize because it hits the exception so frequently.
>
> Obviously getting the underlying boost bug solved would be ideal, but I have no idea what the status of that is (anyone else?). In the interim, one slightly less hacky fix would be to have stan ignore init attempts that fail because of that specific exception. Thoughts?
>
> Oh, and here's some example code (for use from R) demonstrating the timing dramatic difference (there's also a dramatic ESS difference in the same direction):
>
> library(rstan)
> library(CircStats) #for rvm
> set.seed(1)
> y = rvm(1e3,pi,10)
>
> uvm_mod1 = stan_model(model_code=
> "
> data {
>   int N ;
>   vector[N] y ;
> }
> parameters{
>   real<lower=0> kappa ;
> }
> model{
>   kappa ~ lognormal(1,1) ;
>   for(n in 1:N){
>     y[n] ~ von_mises(pi(),kappa) ;
>   }
> }
>
> "
> )
>
> uvm_mod2 = stan_model(model_code=
> "
> data {
>   int N ;
>   vector[N] y ;
> }
> parameters{
>   real<lower=0> kappa ;
> }
> model{
>   kappa ~ lognormal(1,1) ;
>   for(n in 1:N){
>     if(kappa<10){ //use von Mises
>       y[n] ~ von_mises(pi(),kappa) ;
>     }else{ //use normal approximation
>       y[n] ~ normal(pi(),sqrt(1/kappa)) ;
>     }
>   }
> }
>
> "
> )
>
>
> out1 = sampling(
> 	object = uvm_mod1
> 	, data = list(N=length(y),y=y)
> 	, iter = 1e3
> 	, chains = 1
> 	, seed = 1
> )
>
> out2 = sampling(
> 	object = uvm_mod2
> 	, data = list(N=length(y),y=y)
> 	, iter = 1e3
> 	, chains = 1
> 	, seed = 1
> )
>
> get_elapsed_time(out1)
> #I get: chain:1 3.440891 3.652428
> get_elapsed_time(out2)
> #I get: chain:1 179.3448 183.2809
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Stan indexe sfrom 1 so mu[0] doesn't make sense.

Michael Betancourt wrote a nice case study on mixtures you may
want to read --- it's linked from mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> under docs.

- Bob

> On May 12, 2017, at 6:44 AM, Jan Münch <jan.lenna...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey Bob,
> thanks for your help a while ago. I wasn t dealing with this projekt for some time but now I am back to it. I programmed now A mixture of exponentials as you recommended. But I am missing something here with the initialisation of the Parameters. The Programm Fails to initialise the Parameter correctly. Even though I restrict them to be Positiv_ordered and in a simplex... From the Manual I understood that Stan takes care of the bounds of the Parameters in the initialisation. But somehow it doesn t.
>
> In the end the programm is supposed to inference the number of mixture components too. Do you have hint where to start for that. Something like a mixture of a mixture model?
>
> Thanks in advance for your help. Jan
>
> data {
>     int<lower=2> K;                 // number of mixture components
>     int<lower=1> N;                 // number of data points
>     real<lower=0> y[N];             // array observations ever element bigger als 0
> }
> parameters {                        // The parameters we want to inference by via Stan
>     simplex[K] theta;               // mixing proportions
>     positive_ordered[K] mu;         // array rates of mixture components
> }
> model {
>     real ps[K];                     // temp for log component densities
>     //theta ~ uniform(0,1);
>     mu[0] ~ normal(1,1)T[0, ];
>     mu[1] ~ normal(3,3)T[0, ];
>     mu[2] ~ normal(10,10)T[0, ];
>
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>         for (k in 1:K) {
>             ps[k] = log(theta[k])
>             + exponential_lpdf(y[n] | mu[k]);
>         }
>         target += log_sum_exp(ps);
>     }
> }
> """
>
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> Exception thrown at line 14: []: accessing element out of range. index 0 out of range; expecting index to be between 1 and 3; index position = 1mu
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
> Rejecting initial value:
>   Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.
>
> Initialization between (-2, 2) failed after 100 attempts.
>  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
>
>
>
>
> 2017-02-22 19:22 GMT+01:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:
> Sorry---just catching up on some back modeling questions.  It'd be
> really great if others jumped in on some of these.  I'm intentionally
> trying to slow down on answering queries to give others a chance since
> I can no longer keep up.
>
> See inline.
>
> > On Feb 16, 2017, at 2:41 PM, Jan Münch <jan.lenna...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hey Stan Group,
> > I am new to Bayes and try to apply it in the next month to some hidden Markov model inference for proteins. Sofar my toy triexponential decay model does not behave well.
> >  R_hat goes to inifity even though my Priors are to my understanding really restrictive what am I doing wrong here? The rates are seperated by an order of Magnitude. So they should be distinguishabel...
> >
> > regress_code_simple = """
> > data {
> >  int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
> >  real counts[N]; // response variable
> >  real time[N]; // predictor variable
> > }
> > parameters {
> >  real<lower=0> rate1;
> >  real<lower=rate1> rate2;
> >  real<lower=rate2> rate3;
>
> Easier to just do
>
>   positive_ordered[3] rate;
>
> >  real<lower=0> sigma; // standard deviation
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >  real mu[N]; // fitted values
> > for(i in 1:N)
> >  mu[i] = 0.4*exp(-rate1*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate2*time[i])+3.0/10*exp(-rate3*time[i]);
>
> This can be vectorized as follows:
>
>   mu = 0.4 * exp(-rate1 * time)
>      + 0.3 * exp(-rate2 * time)
>      + 0.3 * exp(-rate3 * time));
>
> if you declare time as a vector:
>
>   vector[N] time;
>
> But the bigger problem is that it's not going to be identified because
> you've introduced essentially three regression-like coefficient based
> on the same coefficient and you've given the first two rates plenty of
> latitude.
>
> > }
> > model {
> >  real alpha;
> >  real beta;
> >  alpha = 1.0;
> >  beta  = 1.0;
> >
> >
> >
> >  sigma ~ gamma(alpha,beta);
>
> Much better to just do
>
>   sigma ~ gamma(1, 1);
>
> >
> >  rate1 ~ normal(0,5)T[0,];
> >  rate2 ~ normal(9,5)T[0,];
> >  rate3 ~ normal(95,10)T[0,];
>
> This isn't the right truncations to normalize:
>
>   rate[1] ~ normal(0, 5) T[0, ];
>   rate[2] ~ normal(9, 5) T[rate[1], 0];
>   rate[3] ~ normal(95, 10) T[rate[2], 0];
>
> You can drop the first truncation for efficiency, but you need
> the next two because they depend on parameters.
>
> >  counts ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> But I have no idea why you'd do this.  If you want to define a mixture,
> I'd suggest looking at the mixture modeling section of the manual.  You
> mix the whole distributions, not the means.
>
>
> > }
> > """
> > The error analysis is bad at the beginning and then is fine for some time
>
> The only parameters that look OK here are the rate and sigma.  You may have
> numerical issues in the mu leading to underflow and overflow with the exp(),
> but I'm guessing you really meant to implement a mixture model, not something
> with an odd composite mean.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical Bayesian model and constrained optimization in RStan?! Modeling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical Bayesian model and constrained optimization in RStan?! Modeling
messages.body_plain:
Better yet, I can give you the math:

vector[N] alpha;
real mu;
real sigma;

  alpha ~ normal(mu, sigma);
  mu ~ ...
  sigma ~ ...

as sigma -> 0 and alpha[n] -> mu for all n in 1:N,
the density grows without bound so there's no maximum likelihood
solution.

Greene's probabilityt heory book goes over it in detail and
there's a nice discussion in McKay's book under "EM goes boom".

It's also the reason systems like lme4 use max marginal likelihood
---the max likelihood itself doesn't exist.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Re[2]: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
messages.body_plain:
Usually when you define 95% intervals you're saying that something has a 95% chance of being in that interval. That means 5% of the time you're outside of it.

Your data being outside the 95% intervals of your posterior predictives can also mean that your model isn't doing a good job of explaining your data.

Is it 5% of your data that's outside of the 95% intervals? (this is perfectly normal)

Or is most of your data outside of the intervals? (this can easily happen when you're modeling, and usually means you need to change your model)

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Minima get really finicky even if it's just a minimization you're working on.

It's pretty common to have things that seem like they would have minima, but in the end something crazy happens instead. It's more than just local minima keeping you from the global minima (assuming at least one exists). There can issues with saddlepoint sorts of things for instance (where you're always going down, but limiting to something much larger than the global minima -- this might require the domain of your function to be infinity I forget).

I like running the Stan optimizer on my problems occasionally just to see where it will go. It's one of the easier ways to validate to yourself or your colleagues (or your boss) all that work you did on the Bayesian stuff :D.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] question: can actual data be outside 95%CI of replicated data
messages.body_plain:
In average, 5% of data will be outside of a 95% "CI" obtained directly the true data generating function itself (that is, an interval with 95% probability that a new data point will be inside the interval, given the true data generating function).

So an interval with estimated probability of 95% shouldn't be any better and in fact, if it is "better" than that, then it might be a bad feature... just imagine: you could just say that your CI is the whole line of real numbers (or whatever sample space you have), then your data would be 100% there (and that's why any sensible loss functions would penalize the "size" of the interval since otherwise, you could just choose the full sample space and forget statistics).

> On May 10, 2017, at 6:07 PM, Sean Pinkney <sean.p...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Gelman has a post on lasso regression in Stan. However, I'm wondering if we can do penalized regression with ordinal predictors (paper link) for a logistic regression?

You can't implement the Lasso log density, but it's not continuously
differentiable and we can't find the zero the same way something
like a truncated gradient descent can.

Did you want to enforce some sort of behavior on the coefficients
for the ordinal predictors?  If you're sure of the direction and
ordering of effects, you can use an ordered vector.  Usually you
want K - 1 effects for K categories to aid with identifiability.
Otherwise, you'll be relying very heavily on priors for identifiability.

- Bob

> Basically, I have a number of logistic regressions with ordinal variates which sometimes fail due to low sample on some of the levels of the ordinal variate. So, I could use the ordPens package in R (link). But, the model has a random intercept and random slopes specification with the groups (x6-8 in the example below) so I think a hierarchical penalized logistic regression makes the most sense.
>
> For example
>
> Outcome:
> y ~ binomial
>
> Ordinal predictors
> x1 - income (coded as 1 - 7)
> x2 - age (coded as 1 - 5)
>
> Categorical predictors
> x3 - gender (coded as 0, 1)
>
> Continuous
> x4 - positive real number
> x5 - positive real number
>
> group indicators (observation can be in more than one group)
> x6 - 1,0
> x7 - 1,0
> x8 - 1,0
>
> Thanks for any help or thoughts!

>
> Usually when you define 95% intervals you're saying that something has a 95% chance of being in that interval. That means 5% of the time you're outside of it.
>
> Your data being outside the 95% intervals of your posterior predictives can also mean that your model isn't doing a good job of explaining your data.

It depends on what we're talking about here.  This can happen even
when you're using exactly the same model as was used to generate
the data.  In fact, it'll happen 5% of the time.  In that case, it's
a "bad" draw of data.

This can also happen if the model's misspecified, which is usually
why we run these on real data.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I have been running into a similar issue, and was in the middle of coming up with a similar test case when I came upon this thread.

It looks like (up to additive constants)
log(p(hp | dat1, dat2)) = -n*log(sig1) - dat1^2/2sig1^2 -n*log(sig2) - dat2^2/2sig2^2 -2 log(hp)+log(sig1)-hp*sig1 -2log(hp)+log(sig2)-hp*sig2

log(p(hp_alt | dat1, dat2)) = -n*log(c1_alt*hp_alt) - n*dat1^2/2(c1_alt*hp_alt)^2 -log(c2_alt*hp_alt) - dat2^2/2(c2_alt*hp_alt)^2 +log(c1_alt)-c1_alt +log(c2_alt)-c2_alt

log(p(hp_alt | dat1, dat2)) = -dat1^2/2(c1_alt*hp_alt)^2  - dat2^2/2(c2_alt*hp_alt)^2 -2log(hp_alt)-c1_alt -c2_alt

so if I did my math right, log(p(hp | dat1, dat2)) and log(p(hp_alt | dat1, dat2)) will differ by -n*(log(sig1)+log(sig2))

So, I believe the reparamaterization is equivalent to imposing the gamma(2+n,epsilon) prior from Chung 2015 on the original model?

It also seems like this would be the case with normal distributions as well?  My understanding from the mailing list was that the 'Matt Trick' was just a computational tool to speed up convergence, but working through this example it seems like it is implicitly putting a weakly informative prior on the data as well.

messages.body_plain:
No, looping with multiple calls to an _rng function isn't slow.
Unlike R or Python in their normal interactive forms, Stan compiles
down to C++ where the looping is fast.

Sometimes we can get a bit of boost in speed if there are shared
computations.  This is a *much* bigger deal for parameters, where
vectorizing can cut down the work required for derivatives.  But
there are no derivatives for RNGs.

We do have an issue open for vectorizing the _rng functions, but
it'll just make the code shorter, not faster.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to implement a mixture model of Negative Binomial regression models. I want to use the Dirichlet Process prior to estimate the number of mixture components.
I found this thread (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/d-R7J6MldkQ) with an example code for a hierarchical model, and together with the mixture model example in the docs, I came up with this code:

library(rstan)

model_string <-"
data {
  int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
  int<lower=1> M; //the number of columns in the model matrix
  matrix[N,M] X; //the model matrix
  int y[N]; // observations
  real<lower=0> alpha0 ; // dirichlet prior
}
transformed data {
  vector<lower=0>[K] alpha0_vec;
  for (k in 1:K){
alpha0_vec[k] = alpha0; //symmetric dirichlet prior
}
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta; // mixing proportions
  vector[M] betas[K];
  real<lower=0> sigma[K]; // scales of mixture components
}
model {
  theta ~ dirichlet(alpha0_vec);
  sigma ~ lognormal(0, 2);
  for (k in 1:K)
    betas[k,] ~ normal(0,10);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    real lps[K];
    for (k in 1:K)
      lps[k] = log(theta[k]) + neg_binomial_2_lpmf(y[n] | X[n] * betas[k], sigma[k]);
    target += log_sum_exp(lps);
  }
}"

# toy data
set.seed(123)
N <- 10000
phi <- 1.2
b0 <- -0.5
b1 <- 0.4
X <- data.frame(V=rep(1,N), V1=runif(N), V2=runif(N))
y <- rnbinom(N, size = phi, mu = exp(as.matrix(X) %*% c(1, b0, b1)))

# call stan
m <- stan(model_code = model_string, data = list(X=X, M=ncol(X), K=3, y = y, N = nrow(X), alpha0=0.2), chains=1, cores=1)

If you run this for longer and the n_eff go up proportionally you should be OK.
You'll only find one mode, of course.

>
> I this model specification correct?
>
> When looking at the thetas, theta[1] has a value of 1.0, where the other thetas have zero. Does that mean the optimal number of components is 1?

There's no optimization per se, but that's the posterior mean number
of components.  You could print this to more decimal places and maybe
see that it's not precisely 1.0.

> Actually that would be true here, as the data are generated from a simple NegBin.

Well, that's reassuring at least.

You could also have a stronger prior (wouldn't approximate a DP, but
it may save you from having some bins not have any data).

>  How do I interpret the betas? betas other for components other than the first are meangingless?!

You could run this out to more decimal places.  Probably not exactly meaningless,

If you generated everything from one negative binomial, that's

> ordered mu[K]; // locations of mixture components

an intercept.  Again, I recommend Michael's case study to get some
more understanding of how mixtures work.

You should try upping the target acceptance rate (adapt_delta = 0.95 or 0.99 or something)

messages.body_plain:
Hey Everyone,

This question is relevant to a reply I made at the end of an earlier thread, but I think it was buried. I am fitting a multivariate logistic regression model in rstanarm wherein performance is low but not at floor. Data is also very sparse; there are two conditions and participants contribute only a single binary response to each. I am trying to fit random intercepts and slopes. I have dealt with logistic regression often in the past, but usually in cases where performance was closer to 50% and/or where data was plentiful. Usually the estimates from the model don’t match with basic proportions, but they are not so far off. In this particular instance, the estimates I get from the model differ quite a bit from the raw proportions, more than I am used to seeing. I wanted to double check whether I am doing something unreasonable with my priors that could account for this.

The model I am fitting as follows:

mod = stan_glmer(switched ~ cond + order + choices.s + relprefc1.s + ici.s + bore.s + fat.s + (cond|ID),
                             data = dat,
                             family = binomial,
                             adapt_delta=.999,
                             iter=6000,
                             prior = normal(0, 1.5), # Regularizing prior
                             prior_intercept = normal(-1, 1)) # Encourages grand mean ~5% - ~73%

All predictors are normalized using the scale() function except for cond and order, which are categorical and have been coded as -1 and 1 (following something I read in a post by Andrew). I have applied mildly informative prior to the coefficients and a prior to the intercept (which should be the grand mean) indicative of our belief that overall performance should fall no lower than ~5%.

In doing this, I expected the intercept to be close to the overall mean proportion, but when I check this:

Check the grand mean against the intercept
mean(dat$switched)
plogis(mod$coefficients[1]) # Probability at the mean/centre of all variables

I instead get .15 for the raw proportion and .07 for the back-transformed intercept. Similarly, estimates I calculate for each condition (using posterior_linpred) are generally much lower than the corresponding proportions. Everything seems shifted sharply towards 0. The prior placed on the intercept helps with this situation somewhat. Is this cause for concern? Or is it just the nature of logistic regression near a boundary and with limited data? Am I using inappropriate priors? I have posted some data and code, in case it was helpful.

Cheers!
Jon
